NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The intervention is to install a flow circulation system in dead-end mains that uses the existing pressure in the main to create periodic flow pulses without external energy input, which directly disrupts biofilm formation and removes accumulated biomass. Standard practice relies on periodic flushing with fresh water, which only provides temporary shear stress and consumes disinfectant. The closest existing practice is conventional pipe flushing, but our intervention differs by creating continuous, low-energy flow circulation that maintains disinfectant residual while removing biofilm precursors. This intervention attacks the failure's driving physics by increasing shear stress on pipe walls and removing nutrient-rich stagnant water where biofilm thrives, without requiring additional disinfectant.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the mass transfer coefficient for biofilm detachment: k_d = τ/(μ·ρ), where τ is wall shear stress, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. By creating flow pulses with velocities of 0.3-0.5 m/s (achievable through a pressure-driven circulation system), wall shear stress increases from near-zero (stagnant conditions) to approximately 0.8 Pa, which exceeds the critical shear stress for biofilm detachment (0.3 Pa). This would reduce biofilm accumulation rate by approximately 70-80%, as demonstrated by studies on biofilm response to increased shear stress.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) In-line hydraulic oscillators (procurable from water treatment equipment suppliers, e.g., Red Valve Co.), 2) Low-resistance circulation valves (standard waterworks valves), 3) Connecting pipes (standard PVC or HDPE), 4) Flow control orifice plates (standard components). Materials: All materials must be NSF 61 certified for drinking water contact. Instruments: 1) Pressure gauges (standard waterworks equipment), 2) Flow meters (procurable from water treatment suppliers). Procedure: Install hydraulic oscillator at dead-end main, connect circulation loop with isolation valves, install orifice plate to control flow rate, and program oscillator to activate during low-demand periods (e.g., 2-hour cycles every 12 hours).

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Similar to standard practice (requires excavation and valve installation, but no new infrastructure). Operability: Requires initial programming of oscillator cycles but minimal ongoing intervention. Maintenance: Comparable to standard practice (valve maintenance and oscillator inspection every 6 months). Cost class: Slightly higher initial cost (oscillator equipment) but lower operating cost (no water consumption during circulation cycles). The intervention has similar deployment burden as standard flushing but provides continuous biofilm control rather than periodic disturbance, justifying the slight cost increase through reduced disinfectant consumption and compliance risk.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Install circulation system in a dead-end main with known nitrification history, with a control dead-end main without intervention. Monitor chlorine residual, nitrite, and biofilm density (via swab sampling) at weekly intervals for 90 days during summer conditions. Instruments: Chlorine analyzer, nitrite ion-selective electrode, swab sampling kit with ATP testing. Pass/fail threshold: Intervention main must maintain chlorine residual >1.0 mg/L and nitrite <0.1 mg/L (regulatory limit) while showing 50% reduction in biofilm ATP compared to control. Duration: 90 days. Kill criterion: If intervention main fails to maintain chlorine residual or if nitrite exceeds regulatory limit at any point, the intervention is falsified.
